How can a machine tell people, through touch, what it knows, what it doesn’t, and when it might be wrong?

I’m Mihir Sharma, a designer turned HCI researcher working on haptic interfaces, accessibility for blind and low-vision people and trust in AI. I study how AI systems should talk to people through vibration: which answers a buzz can carry, how a wearable should limit its false alarms, and how a system can show that it is unsure.

I came to research through design. For my MFA at the College for Creative Studies in Detroit, I built TactileGrip, climbing holds that beep as a hand gets close and vibrate when it grips. In a preliminary gym evaluation, ten blindfolded sighted expert climbers each got further up the route than with verbal guidance alone, and their partners gave no hold-level directions. That result made me ask what else touch could carry.

My evidence so far comes from two kinds of work. From 2022 to 2024, as a designer, I ran studies with people: 20 interviews and a gym evaluation for TactileGrip, a 40-person VR study and 12 co-design sessions with farmers. Since 2026 I have built prototypes and analysed public data from blind users and wearables, and each paper ships with code that rebuilds every number in it.

Since 2026 I have worked on that question as an independent researcher. Three of my papers are under review, at ACM IUI, ACM CHIIR and PACM IMWUT, and two more are in progress. I am applying to PhD programs for 2027, to take this work from datasets and simulations to studies with blind and low-vision people.

From design to research

  1. 2022–23 · MFA, Detroit

    DetroTune

    With four classmates I built a VR journey through Detroit’s techno history for the Detro Tune exhibition at Ars Electronica. It was my first study with people: our 40 participants remembered more than with video learning.

  2. 2023–24 · MFA thesis

    TactileGrip

    I built climbing holds that guide a blind climber’s hand with sound and vibration. In a preliminary test with ten blindfolded sighted climbers, partners gave no hold-level directions while the holds guided the hand. Touch had taken over a job the voice used to do.

  3. 2024 · General Motors

    Vangard

    I designed how a self-driving car tells passengers what it is about to do. It left me with a research question: how firmly should a machine say what it intends?

  4. 2026–now · Independent research

    Touch and AI

    After a year at Ecosphere Organics researching bio-waste materials with built-in sensors, I turned TactileGrip’s question toward AI: which answers a vibration can carry, how a watch should limit its false buzzes, and how to tell whether people use a felt confidence cue.

Research: Haptic Human–AI Interaction

All papers are sole-authored. Papers under anonymous review are listed by title and venue only; preprints, code and prototypes are available on request. In every paper I fix the analysis rules before opening the test data, include a script that recomputes every reported number, say what has and has not been tested with people, and disclose how I used AI tools, including Claude.

ACM IUI 2027 Poster · submitted Oct 2026, under review

Can a Buzz Answer That? How Much of What Blind People Ask a Visual Assistant Fits a Vibration Vocabulary

Mihir Sharma

Blind people use visual assistant apps to ask questions about photos they take, and the answer always comes back as speech, even when it is just “yes”, a number, a colour or “I can’t tell from this photo”. I designed a small set of vibration rhythms for these answers and measured how many real questions they could cover. Of 8,000 held-out questions from blind people (the VizWiz dataset), 15.5% could be answered with a rhythm, and 26.8% more with a felt “can’t tell”. A real vision–language model, run on the same questions, gave a confident answer on 20% of the photos people had marked unanswerable. So an assistant must first be able to say it can’t tell.

  • Data32,842 questions from the VizWiz dataset, asked by blind people; 8,000 held out for testing
  • BuiltFelt Answers, the offline phone prototype pictured, with Ask, Learn, Test and Check modes
  • ChecksOne script rebuilds every number, figure and the poster (49 number checks); the model analysis plan was written before running the model

No one has felt the rhythms in a study yet.

PACM IMWUT Journal · submitted Nov 2026, under review

TrueTap: Budgeting How Often a Smartwatch Buzzes You by Mistake

Mihir Sharma

Smartwatches can spot activities such as eating and buzz to nudge the wearer, but every false buzz costs attention and trust. TrueTap lets each wearer set a budget for false buzzes, for example one per hour, and tunes the detector on calibration data so that only a small, chosen share of wearers go over it. This guarantee holds when new wearers resemble the ones it was tuned on. On day-long wrist recordings from 151 adults, 3.7% of wearers went over budget, within the method’s 9.8% bound, compared with 7.6% with a fixed setting. I tested it on three more public datasets and report where the guarantee breaks.

  • DataFour public wearable datasets: CAPTURE-24, WISDM, HARTH and Daphnet
  • BuiltA Python library and a browser runtime
  • ChecksRerunning CAPTURE-24 from its raw 20 Hz recordings reproduced all 97,920 result rows; a script rechecks every number in the paper (212 checks)

It has not yet run on a watch or with users.

ACM CHIIR 2027 Short Paper · submitted Oct 2026, under review

Material Confidence: Which Outcomes Can Tell Felt from Seen AI Confidence?

Mihir Sharma

Some AI assistants show how confident they are, and people use that to decide when to follow them. If the confidence were felt as a vibration instead of seen on a screen, how would a study tell whether people use it? I re-analysed a public dataset of 35,670 decisions people made with AI advice, then simulated the planned study many times to choose its measure before collecting any data. The usual measure, appropriate reliance, would need about 1,820 participants. A measure of how closely reliance follows the AI’s confidence detected use of the cue in 99% of simulated 96-person studies, assuming people read the vibration correctly 80% of the time.

  • DataHAIID, a public dataset of human–AI decisions; 200 simulated studies for each sample size
  • BuiltA web study app with pilot and device-test modes, band firmware and a study protocol ready for preregistration
  • ChecksEvery input and script is listed with its SHA-256 hash; browser tests cover the full study flow

The study has not been run.

Manuscript Full paper · in preparation

SenseShift: Adaptive AI‑to‑Tactile Communication for Blind and Low-Vision People

Mihir Sharma

A vision–language model can describe a street to a blind pedestrian, but an assistant also has to decide what is worth an interruption, and say it without taking over the person’s hearing. SenseShift predicts how close each object will come, sends only what matters, and turns each message into a short pattern on six vibration pods around the forearm. I built it in Python and in the browser and tested it on 10,500 generated walks. On 1,000 held-out walks it warned of 90.0% of hazards one to five seconds ahead, and only 8.7% of its messages were about distractors. Announcing the nearest object warned of 71.3%, with 63.7% about distractors.

Grew out of TactileGrip.

  • Data10,500 generated walks, split into development, selection, held-out and stress sets
  • BuiltA Python reference system and a browser platform that make identical decisions on 5,753 benchmark frames; study apps and band firmware
  • PlannedThree studies with 12–24 blind and low-vision adults, fully specified

The evidence is computational. The band is designed but not assembled, and the studies have not run.

Work in progress Short paper

Feel the Frame: Touch-Guided Camera Aiming for Blind Users of Visual AI Assistants

Mihir Sharma

Before a visual assistant can answer, a blind user has to take a usable photo, which is hard without seeing the screen. Feel the Frame checks each camera frame for five problems (too dark, too bright, blurry, obstructed or badly framed), lets the phone fix what it can, such as turning on the torch, and otherwise gives one vibration cue at a time on a four-motor sleeve. It stops and hands control back when a correction isn’t working. I trained and tested the five detectors on 7,750 photos taken by blind people; on held-out photos they reach an AUROC of .66 to .95.

  • Data7,750 VizWiz photos taken by blind people, split before any fitting into 3,862 for building and 3,888 held out
  • BuiltAn Android web prototype; a sleeve design with an ESP32-C3 and four coin motors (about $32 in parts) and host-tested firmware
  • ChecksA full rerun from the raw photos reproduces every result (105 number checks)

The sleeve has not been built or worn.

Design work

MFA Thesis College for Creative Studies, 2023–24

TactileGrip: Real-time Sensor-Embedded Climbing Holds for Non-Visual Route Navigation

Mihir Sharma, Predrag K. Nikolić

Thesis Select Award · UX Design Award nominee, New Talent, 2024

Blind climbers usually depend on a sighted guide calling out holds from the ground, and that voice fades with height and gym noise. TactileGrip puts the guidance inside the holds: a beep that speeds up as the hand gets closer, a vibration when it grips, a hold shape that points toward the next hold, and star-shaped holds that announce progress aloud. I shaped it through 20 interviews with blind and low-vision climbers, guides, coaches and gym staff, then built and tested the holds. In a preliminary gym evaluation, all ten blindfolded sighted expert climbers completed more of the route with TactileGrip than with verbal guidance alone (p = .002), and their partners gave no hold-level directions.

  • Methods20 interviews; an autoethnographic climb; a blindfolded workshop; ergonomics tests that cut two of three hold forms; two rounds of voice-only usability tests; a preliminary gym evaluation (N = 10)
  • BuiltArduino Nano holds with an ultrasonic sensor read every 50 ms, a vibration motor and 3D-printed forms

Led to SenseShift.

General Motors Sponsored studio, 2024

Vangard: Autonomous Mobility for Chongqing in 2040

Mihir Sharma (UX), with an exterior and an interior designer

Shortlisted by GM; refined with GM designers over the summer

A 12-week studio, sponsored by General Motors, imagining self-driving cars for Chongqing in 2040, a dense and vertical city. I was the UX designer in a team of three. I designed how the car tells passengers what it is doing and what it will do next: route-intent messages, an always-visible automation status and override controls, across more than 45 infotainment wireframes. GM shortlisted the project, and we were one of two teams invited to refine it with GM designers over the summer.

Led to Intent Through Touch.

Ars Electronica Festival Linz, 2023

DetroTune: Motown Techno, Detroit’s Music History in VR

Mihir Sharma, Raghunath Rajasekar, Siddhi Sakhare, Mahsa Khoshkbar Foroushan, Sara Fallahi

Exhibited at Ars Electronica Festival and Detroit Month of Design

Detro Tune was the College for Creative Studies exhibition at Ars Electronica 2023, and Motown Techno was our team’s piece in it: a virtual-reality journey through Detroit’s downtown and its techno music. I designed the spatial experience and built it in Unity, with 3D sound and motion feedback. In our mixed-methods study with 40 people, participants remembered more and were more engaged than with video-based learning.

  • MethodsMixed-methods study, N = 40: VR against video-based learning
  • BuiltUnity, spatial audio, motion feedback

UX Design Awards Nominee, Berlin, 2023

Farmacy: AI for Agricultural Resilience

Mihir Sharma

A farming app co-designed with smallholder farmers and grocers over 12 sessions. It brings field mapping, crop recommendations and profit forecasting into one place, with voice-first input for people who read little. I did the field research, designed how the system fits together, and designed the voice and visual interface.

  • MethodsField studies in low-literacy communities; 12 co-design sessions with farmers and retailers
